Daniel’s CNN–light-cone analogy is suggestive, but it quietly equates *finite signal speed* with *computational locality*, and those are not the same thing. A light cone limits causal influence, yet many physical theories still require globally coupled *constraint solves* at each “time step” in any straightforward simulation: incompressible fluids enforce ∇·v=0 via a Poisson solve, electrostatics/gravity often reduce to elliptic equations, and gauge constraints can couple the whole domain even when the underlying dynamics is relativistic. This is why the “soft vs rigid / compressible vs incompressible” update you added is so important: it’s basically the same point in numerical analysis terms—hyperbolic PDEs look like local stencil updates (CNN-like), while elliptic constraints create nonlocal computational work. The deepest question isn’t “is there 超距作用?”, but “what parts of physics are hyperbolic local updates versus global constraints, and what representation makes the constraints cheap?”

The complexity argument also smuggles in a worst-case algorithm as if it were a law of nature: “infinite light speed ⇒ O(V²)” resembles naïve all-pairs interaction, but even with true long-range forces you can often do far better (e.g., [Fast multipole method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_multipole_method) brings many N-body interactions close to linear-time under structure assumptions). Conversely, strict locality doesn’t guarantee cheapness if you need very long time horizons, high accuracy, or if small local errors cascade—so “O(V)” is not the whole story. If Daniel wants to keep the “god’s simulator” framing, a sharper version would separate (i) locality/causality, (ii) *algorithmic compressibility* (can interactions be summarized hierarchically?), and (iii) *stiffness/conditioning* (does the problem force tiny steps or global solves?).

On “continuous CNN,” Daniel is circling a lineage that already exists under different names: continuous convolutions, wavelets, and—more directly for PDE-like “fields”—neural operators that learn mappings between function spaces (e.g., the [Fourier Neural Operator](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.08895)). If the goal is to mirror physics, it may help to anchor the analogy in “local update rules on a lattice” (the [cellular automaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cellular_automaton) tradition) plus known bounds on how fast influence can spread in local quantum systems (the computational analog of a light cone appears in [Lieb–Robinson bounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieb%E2%80%93Robinson_bounds)). That framing would also clarify the “Planck low-pass filter” idea: a cutoff is a standard move in effective field theory, but it’s less “the universe is blurred” than “a theory’s degrees of freedom change with scale,” which is a subtler—and more interesting—claim than mere bandwidth limitation.
